    WR Brandon Aiyuk reportedly clears waivers after finally being released by 49ers, would like to sign soon

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yahoo

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After finally being released by the San Francisco 49ers, veteran wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk has cleared waivers, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter, who also reported Tuesday that Aiyuk would like to sign with a fresh team soon.
    • He's expected to attract interest from a few teams, including the Washington Commanders, per Schefter.
    • In a recent development, the Niners releasing Aiyuk marked the end of a months-long standoff between the team and player.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After finally being released by the San Francisco 49ers, veteran wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk has cleared waivers, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter, who also reported Tuesday that Aiyuk would like to sign with a fresh team soon.

    He's expected to attract interest from a few teams, including the Washington Commanders, per Schefter.

    In a recent development, the Niners releasing Aiyuk marked the end of a months-long standoff between the team and player. Aiyuk missed the entire 2025 NFL season after recovering from a knee injury he suffered in 2024, just months after signing a four-year, $120 million extension with the team. He suffered a torn ACL and MCL in late October 2024 and hasn't played a snap in the league since.

    Sources indicate that san Francisco had a two-week roster exemption for Aiyuk. It expired on Monday, and as a result, the franchise opted to release Aiyuk, giving both the team and the wide receiver a fresh start.

    According to recent reports, aiyuk was subject to waivers, but upon clearing them, he's reportedly a free agent. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported on Monday that a spot on the Commanders' practice squad is the likeliest next step for Aiyuk.

    After being placed on the physically unable to perform list, reports later emerged that Aiyuk failed to participate in team meetings and the Niners were frustrated with the "lack of communication." Eventually, he was placed on the Reserve/Left Squad list in December 2025 due to his continued absence and lack of communication with the team.

    Industry observers note that aiyuk was officially reinstated from the Reserve/Left Squad list on Nov. 9, at which time the 49ers were granted a two-week roster exemption to decide if they wanted to release him, trade him or add him to the 53-man roster. The reinstatement was the first step toward Aiyuk's eventual release.

    Aiyuk's breakup with the Niners is no surprise. Leading up to the 2025 season, reports surfaced that guarantees in his contract were voided amid growing frustrations between the organization and the veteran wideout.

    Then in January, 49ers GM John Lynch officially acknowledged the impending divorce between the two sides, stating in his end-of-season news conference, "I think it's safe to say he's played his last snap with the 49ers.".

    Sources indicate that aiyuk is 28 and hasn't played since Week 7 of the 2024 season. Before his injury, he had spent his entire five-year career with the 49ers.

    Recent findings suggest that san Francisco drafted him with the 25th pick in the 2020 NFL Draft. He had his breakout season in 2022, finishing with 1,015 yards and eight touchdowns. Aiyuk returned in 2023 and improved, finishing with 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns.

    The Niners have turned to Deebo Samuel, Mike Evans and Keenan Allen in the passing game in Aiyuk's absence, with promising rookie De'Zhaun Stribling expected to return from injury soon.

    It has been revealed that if Aiyuk joins Washington, the Commanders will look to get him up to speed as No. 1 wide receiver Terry McLaurin has been ruled out for the season due to a torn ACL. Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams have picked up the slack, but Washington could use Aiyuk if he can play close to his pre-injury level.

    10 stocks we like better than Alnylam Pharmaceuticals ›.

    On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, Alnylam (ALNY +5.53%) unveiled full-year transthyretin (TTR, a transport protein involved in rare amyloid diseases) product revenue will land at the low end of its $4.2 billion to $4.5 billion guidance range. While sales of core treatments continue to grow, slower prescription conversion for key heart medicine AMVUTTRA (vutrisiran) and impending federal reimbursement changes present near-term hurdles. The tech giant is relying on trial expansions and pipeline diversification to protect its long-term strategy.

    Three things management remarked stand out.

    Recent findings suggest that management expanded its sales team to reach non-specialist physicians, but converting doctor visits into fresh prescriptions is taking longer than expected. Community doctors care for fewer amyloidosis patients and have entrenched habits, so leadership expects no material top-line revenue from the field force expansion in 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier diagnosis and broader use of background heart medications across the industry are lowering cardiovascular event rates in clinical trials. To keep the TRITON-CM phase III trial for next-generation drug nucresiran statistically robust without delaying its planned 2030 commercial launch, management increased enrollment to 2,250 patients.

    A proposed federal rule change targeting the 340B drug discount program (a federal program allowing safety-net hospitals to purchase outpatient drugs at discounted prices) may prompt health systems to alter purchasing pathways. Because customer responses remain uncertain, management is withholding next year's product revenue forecast until mid-February.

    Sources indicate that commercial product sales in rare genetic conditions are funding a broader neurological pipeline, and leadership is not hiding its urgency to convert expanded physician outreach into new patient starts. Differentiated trial data and high quarterly treatment adherence protect the core business as leadership manages evolving Medicare policies and pricing discipline across hospital networks.

    Advancing phase III clinical trials and entering newly introduced therapeutic categories like Huntington's disease (a rare, inherited neurological disorder) expand long-term commercial reach, while proprietary delivery technology reinforces competitive position as Alnylam pursues multi-franchise growth over the coming decade.

    Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).
    • Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in?
    • First, let's remember how we got here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).

    Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

    First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout rapidly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

    The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

    Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:.

    This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

    For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

    According to recent reports, the following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

    Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

    The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

    According to recent reports, the major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

    That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

    One key clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

    Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

    We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

    The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

    From here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see fresh highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

    Tech Report: This AI Chip Stock Just Crashed 38% on a Memory Shortage Warning. Its Filings Flagged the Risk Months Ago

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ambarella (AMBA -19.96%) shares plummeted 38% to $27 in after-hours trading Tuesday after the chipmaker warned that a worldwide memory shortage is hurting demand for its products.
    • Ambarella makes low-power chips that run artificial intelligence directly on devices such as security cameras, car safety systems, drones and dashcams.
    • But what spooked investors were the projections: For the fourth quarter, which ends Jan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 24, 2026 at 6:27PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Ambarella ›.

    It has been revealed that ambarella (AMBA -19.96%) shares plummeted 38% to $27 in after-hours trading Tuesday after the chipmaker warned that a worldwide memory shortage is hurting demand for its products. Nasdaq halted trading in the stock at 4:01 p.m. ET ahead of the news.

    Ambarella makes low-power chips that run artificial intelligence directly on devices such as security cameras, car safety systems, drones and dashcams. Revenue for the third quarter, which ended Oct. 31, rose 6% to $115.2 million, while adjusted earnings rose to $0.28 per share from $0.27 a year earlier.

    But what spooked investors were the projections: For the fourth quarter, which ends Jan. 31, Ambarella expects revenue of $70 million to $75 million. That's a drop of 35% to 39% from the quarter it just reported.

    According to recent reports, "The unprecedented rise in memory prices and the scarcity of memory supply we previously highlighted has intensified and is causing many customers to reduce their outlooks," CEO Fermi Wang noted in the release. He added that third-quarter revenue landed at the low end of the company's guidance range because consumer device sales came in below expectations.

    Ambarella doesn't make memory, but almost every device that uses its chips also needs memory chips. When memory becomes scarce and expensive, the camera and car electronics makers that buy from Ambarella build fewer products or delay them, and they order fewer Ambarella chips.

    Recent findings suggest that ambarella isn't the only firm feeling it this week. Hewlett Packard Enterprise CEO Antonio Neri mentioned on Monday's earnings call that he expects memory supply to stay constrained until at least the second half of 2028. On Tuesday, HP Inc. said in its earnings release that it is "taking steps to address memory and storage cost pressures.".

    Recent findings suggest that ambarella guided for adjusted operating expenses of $57.5 million to $59.5 million in the fourth quarter, with an adjusted gross margin of 59% to 60.25%. At the midpoints, that works out to about $43 million in gross profit against roughly $58.5 million in expenses, resulting in an adjusted operating loss of about $15 million. Using the company's third-quarter figures, which leave out stock-based compensation and acquisition costs the same way its guidance does, Ambarella earned an adjusted operating profit of about $11 million.

    Sources indicate that the company expects to keep its overall spending roughly level even as revenue drops, and it has the cash to do so. It ended the quarter with $282.8 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, up from $272.3 million three months earlier.

    In a recent development, ambarella had been flagging the problem for months. Its March annual report listed memory shortages as a possibility. By its June quarterly report, it said there "have been tightening supply conditions in the memory market." In September's quarterly report, it added that tighter memory supply "could have an impact on" customers' demand for its products.

    According to recent reports, the earnings release 8-K that came out a day earlier didn't mention memory specifically at all. It forecast third-quarter revenue of $115 million to $124 million. Ambarella came in at $115.2 million, the bottom of that range.

    According to recent reports, wang tried to separate the shortage from the long-term story. Memory problems "do not have an impact on our very positive secular growth outlook for edge AI," he stated, and he expects the organization's fiscal 2028, which begins in February, "to be a growth year.".

    Sources indicate that that's a claim worth assessing. Ambarella says many of its customers are lowering their outlooks while memory stays scarce and expensive, and if HPE's view holds, that may not ease until at least the second half of 2028. Wang also noted edge AI revenue hit a record in the third quarter, so the demand for AI on devices is real. The question is how long the memory squeeze keeps it from turning into sales.

    Recent findings suggest that for investors in semiconductor stocks, Ambarella's warning is a reminder that the AI boom comes at a cost to companies outside the data center, with the same memory demand that's filling orders for AI servers draining supply from smaller device makers. Until Ambarella shows its revenue can recover, its stock is likely to trade on headlines about memory prices (as HPE and Dell did on Tuesday), and buyers looking for a turnaround in AI may want to wait for next quarter's guidance.

    Berkshire Hit a Record High While AI Power Stocks Sold Off. Here’s What That Says About Where Energy Money Is Going.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 24, 2026 at 6:42PM EST.
    • 10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›.
    • Recent findings suggest that over the past three months, Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.73%)(BRKB +0.85%) is up roughly 15% as of this writing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 24, 2026 at 6:42PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›.

    Recent findings suggest that over the past three months, Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.73%)(BRKB +0.85%) is up roughly 15% as of this writing. By comparison, Bloom Energy (BE -6.98%) and Caterpillar (CAT -1.17%), both headline-grabbing artificial intelligence (AI) energy plays, are down 29% and 38%, respectively. Investors aren't giving up on the companies that provide energy for AI, but they may be shifting toward more conservative investments. Here's what you need to know.

    Artificial intelligence is really just a fancy computer program. Without electricity, it can't exist. But AI uses a tremendous amount of power, resulting in consumer backlash against the data centers that host it. This is why investors have been so attracted to Bloom Energy and Caterpillar.

    Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. These factory-produced items can be placed wherever they are needed to provide off-grid power. Caterpillar, while best known for its heavy earth-moving equipment, also makes generators that provide off-grid power. However, given the backlash against AI, investor enthusiasm for AI stocks has diminished, and these stocks have fallen alongside the broader AI trade despite still-high expectations for power demand.

    Meanwhile, Berkshire Hathaway's shares have been on the rise. That is at least partly a flight-to-safety trade. Berkshire Hathaway is a giant conglomerate with businesses ranging from insurance to homebuilding, and much in between. It also has more than $370 billion in cash sitting on its balance sheet to cushion it against a market downturn. That cash also provides it with the ability to buy if a bear market opens up attractive investment opportunities.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Industry observers note that that's a good start, but there's another small wrinkle here. Over the last three months, Southern Company (SO +1.07%), a large regulated U.S. utility, is up nearly 5%, and Kinder Morgan (KMI +1.67%), a large North American pipeline operator, is down just 2%. These businesses will both be integral to powering AI. They aren't as exciting as Bloom Energy or Cat, but that's the point right now. Investors are looking for a safe haven as AI enthusiasm hits a road bump and are shifting toward boring, reliable businesses.

    Recent findings suggest that notably, Southern offers a reliable 3.2% dividend yield, while Kinder Morgan's yield is 3.9%. Berkshire Hathaway doesn't pay a dividend; however, two of its largest divisions are its utility and energy segments. Add that to the rest of the tech giant's owned business portfolio and its large collection of publicly traded stocks, and you have diversification along with continued exposure to the growing demand for electricity. This is not a small matter, given that electricity demand increased by 10% between 2005 and 2025 and is projected to grow by 60% between 2025 and 2045.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    According to recent reports, basically, Berkshire Hathaway could offer the best of both worlds. You own a diversified and financially strong company that is prepared to take advantage of a bear market. And you continue to have exposure to AI's growing appetite for power. All in one investment. Investors may not be dumping AI power companies; they may just be getting more selective and conservative.

    Sources indicate that the caveat here is that Berkshire Hathaway is now trading near all-time highs. However, the company has been buying back its own stock over the last two quarters, which it has historically done only when it believes the stock is trading below its intrinsic value. While it probably isn't fair to suggest Berkshire Hathaway is a deep-value opportunity, if you are looking for a safer way to play long-term energy demand from AI, the company itself thinks its stock is attractive. It's probably worth a deep dive, even if you only end up putting it on your wish list.

    10 stocks we like better than Domino's Pizza ›.

    Industry observers note that picture a local franchise owner managing a dozen units across a city. She relies on a centralized supply chain that delivers dough and ingredients overnight, a digital ordering system that processes over 85% of her transactions, and a consistent, predictable royalty structure. This is the operational engine behind Domino's Pizza (DPZ +0.36%), a global food giant that has scaled to over 22,700 locations since its founding in 1960. As of Nov. 19, 2026, the stock trades at $352.12, having returned -12% over the past year as the business navigates a complex environment of slowing consumer discretionary spending and intense competition.

    Recent findings suggest that our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns Domino's Pizza an overall Superscore of 85 out of 100, placing it in the Strong category. The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a company's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39). An 85 places the company in the top ~4% of every company we score. This article pairs the reasons the score is high with the risks that keep it from rising further, so you can decide whether the business fits your investment goals.

    The manufacturer maintains a high return on net tangible assets, which measures how much profit the business earns for every dollar of its hard tangible assets. This efficiency means that even moderate revenue growth can translate into meaningful returns for shareholders, partially offsetting the risks of a higher valuation multiple in a competitive market.

    This stock warrants a closer look if...

    You may want to keep researching before buying if...

    The Superscore is one data-driven signal worth investigating; please weigh it against your own research, risk tolerance, and long-term financial goals before making any investment decisions.

    It has been revealed that domino's asset-light, franchise-heavy business model has been a recipe for success over the past few decades. Since 2006, the pizza stock has delivered more than 2,600% gains for investors as the tech giant expanded its geographic footprint and leveraged technology to serve customers more efficiently. It has grown its dividend for 12 consecutive years, now paying out 2.23%. These characteristics are all reasons Domino's has been a solid defensive investment, but where could the stock go from here?

    Domino's next phase of growth will likely rhyme with its first. Geographic expansion, this time internationally, will be critical. The company already operates in more than 90 international markets, with more international stores than U.S. locations. Markets like China and India still offer significant room to expand. But international growth also adds operational and financial complexity. Digital leadership will also continue to drive DPZ's performance. The company that brought us the "pizza tracker" now relies heavily on digital orders, which typically carry higher average tickets and lower error rates. Continued innovation and investment in this area will be notable for its next five years of growth.

    In a recent development, domino's provides a tantalizing combination of value, convenience, and consistency. And growth is still on the table: According to Mordor Intelligence, the pizza foodservice market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 10% through 2031, with Asia-Pacific expected to grow even faster. Meanwhile, continued share buybacks and dividend payments will reward patient investors while they wait -- no tracker required.

    Recent findings suggest that this is an important milestone and a sign of our progress towards the full earnings and cash potential of the business. And earlier this month, we received FDA clearance for MiniMed Fit, our first tubeless insulin pump. Fit brings our therapy to people who prefer a patch pump and opens an important new growth opportunity for MiniMed.

We believe this progress positions us well for the next phase of MiniMed's growth. Now let me spend a few minutes on our U.S. business. We delivered the solid high single-digit growth we expected and the strong demand we described last quarter continues to build.

    Latest pumps sold increased more than 30% year-over-year, helped by the continued rollout of the MiniMed Flex, including expanded coverage for people on Medicare and the launch of Flex with the Instinct sensor. The majority of U.S. Flex new pumps sold continues to come from patients who are new to pump therapy or who switched from a competitor, showing that Flex is expanding our reach beyond existing MiniMed customers.

    With Flex, patients can now choose a smaller, more discreet durable pump that they control from an app paired with our SmartGuard adaptive algorithm with 2 modern sensors, Simplera and Instinct. During Q2, we held several regional Flex training programs across the United States and the number of upcoming MiniMed prescribers increased 36% sequentially. These results reinforce our confidence in the strength and long-term opportunity of our U.S. business. Turning to international. We delivered another strong quarter. Growth was broad-based. In Western Europe, new pumps sold grew more than 20% year-over-year, reinforcing the strength of demand and our confidence in durable growth across the region.

    We continue to benefit from fresh products, our investments to increase sensor supply and growing adoption of automated insulin delivery in markets where adoption remains relatively low. Several of our largest European markets performed especially well with double-digit growth in the U.K., France and Spain. And Germany delivered its highest revenue growth in 2 years. In the U.K., Instinct gave patients sensor choice and supported strong pump demand. In France, growing use of Simplera drove strong CGM growth and supported pump sales. In Spain, we delivered more than 20% revenue growth despite increased competitive activity. And in Germany, strong prescription demand and solid sales execution drove the improvement.

    These results give us confidence in our international business as we begin the next phase of the Flex rollout. Last week, we launched MiniMed Flex with Simplera in Western Europe, with Flex now available in 9 European countries following a successful early customer experience phase across 5 markets. The initial interest from patients and physicians has been strong. Flex with Instinct received CE Mark last month and remains on track to launch in our fiscal fourth quarter. Together, these releases give people more choice in pumps and sensors and give us more ways to meet the needs and preferences of people living with diabetes.

    According to recent reports, we believe we are well positioned to launch Flex into a strong and growing Western European business with strong pump demand, more sensor options and established commercial and market access infrastructure. Our ability to commercialize at scale is an important advantage. Simplera is now available in over 50 countries and Instinct in 14, supported by our reimbursement capabilities, clinical relationships and customer support infrastructure across the region. Together, these capabilities and our expanding product portfolio give us confidence in a long runway for durable international growth. Now let me turn to our innovation pipeline. Last quarter, I told you we were not launching individual products. We were building the next generation of MiniMed, one company, every option, one ecosystem.

    Three months later, several of those programs have taken another crucial leap forward. More importantly, we continue to deliver on the roadmap we laid out when we separated from Medtronic with products moving from development to pivotal trials, from trials to submission to approval and from approval to commercialization. Let me start with MiniMed Fit. Earlier this month, we received FDA clearance for Fit several months ahead of expectations and just a couple of months after our submission in late August. As a result, we now expect to accelerate our early customer experience phase in Q4 this fiscal year and shift left the full U.S. commercial launch to spring of 2027. MiniMed Fit is a major strategic milestone for MiniMed.

    It has been revealed that it brings our differentiated therapy platform to a new segment for MiniMed and the fastest-growing segment of insulin delivery. We began preparing for commercialization ahead of clearance, building our manufacturing capability, market access and commercial infrastructure in parallel with the regulatory process. That work continues as we prepare for launch. We expect to have enough capacity to support approximately 20,000 patients in the first year of launch. And we designed our manufacturing network to scale significantly as the launch expands. Fit is simply not another patch pump. It's the first of its kind, designed from the ground up with what patch customers need.

    Patients have told us they want 3 things from a tubeless pump: longer wear, more insulin capacity and better automation. Fit is everything a tubeless system should be. Fit pairs up to 7 days of wear with a 300-unit insulin reservoir, so patients can change patches less often without giving up insulin capacity. It's app-controlled and designed to be waterproof. It keeps a persistent Bluetooth connection, so patients don't have to re-pair every fresh patch with their phone, and it can be worn in multiple places on the body. Fit also works with Simplera and Instinct and runs our SmartGuard algorithm. Until now, they've had to trade off one against another. With Fit, they don't.

    It has been revealed that that means fewer changes and less to think about with strong glucose control in a system that's easy to live with. We believe customers will feel the difference. And Fit is not the endpoint. It's designed to take wireless software updates, giving consumers a seamless path to Vivera, our fully closed-loop algorithm when it becomes available. As we discussed last quarter, Vivera is designed to eliminate carb counting or meal announcements while still delivering strong outcomes above the ADA guidelines of 70% time in range. We have fully enrolled our pivotal trial and are in the final stages of data collection.

    In a recent development, based on our current timelines, we expect to submit Vivera to the FDA and report pivotal trial data in the first half of calendar year 2027, and we remain on track for a U.S. launch in the second half of calendar '27. Across the industry, most new competitor algorithms are built for one patient population and one style of use. That leaves patients and clinicians making trade-offs: simplicity or performance, hands-free or hands-on, type 1 or type 2, adult or pediatric, durable pump or patch pump. Our goal with Vivera was not to solve one of these trade-offs, it was to eliminate them. Diabetes is not one-size-fits-all. Needs differ between type 1 and type 2 and between adults and children.

    And even within these groups, they vary widely and change over time. Nowhere is this clearer than at mealtime. Carb counting is the last manual task in automated insulin delivery. And for 25 years, it has quietly decided who can use a pump. Other systems treat it as a switch, either you announce every meal or you give up control. Vivera treats it as a dial. Patients who want peak performance can choose to enter their meals. Patients who don't want to count carbs at all can skip it, and Vivera still delivers strong glucose control. Patients choose how to be involved at every meal, and that choice can change from one day to the next.

    According to recent reports, vivera is also designed for type 1 and type 2, children and adults at launch. We expect to offer it on Flex and Fit as a seamless over-the-air patch, so patients can choose a durable pump or patch pump without giving up algorithm performance. This flexibility in one algorithm took more than a decade of R&D, clinical research and simulation tools to build. The better the app automation, the broader the addressable population that will adopt AID therapy. Think of Vivera like a full self-driving car. The car drives, but you can take the wheel anytime you want, and that's exactly why people trust it enough to let it drive. Vivera works the same way.

    It has been revealed that it handles insulin every 5 minutes, day and night. When you want even tighter control at a meal, you can enter carbs and take the wheel. When you don't, Vivera keeps driving. Other fully closed-loop systems work like a switch. Once it's on, you're a passenger. You only get what that algorithm can do on its own. And when something goes wrong, there's very little you can do about it. With Vivera, you never have to choose between letting go and getting the outcomes you deserve. Our sensor pipeline is moving too. Through our partnership with Abbott, we are integrating a dual glucose-ketone sensor into the MiniMed ecosystem.

    We expect to be the first to bring glucose and ketone monitoring together in one app with the sensor expected to launch with our new pumps next summer. Step back and the story isn't any single milestone. It's the momentum across the portfolio. A year ago, these programs were in development. Today, they are in pivotal trials, winning approvals and reaching patients. We're building the most complete platform for people who take insulin: Smart MDI, durable pump, patch pump and a choice of sensors, all connected by one algorithm and one digital ecosystem. And increasingly, we are no longer just building that platform. We are putting it in the hands of patients.

Flex, Fit, Go, Vivera and our sensor pipeline will expand the number of patients we serve from here.     I mean it's -- I think in consumer electronics, if you look at a watch, that's why you've got a small watch and a bigger watch. People sometimes pick the bigger watch. It's not always the case that you want something small if the functionality that you're going after, the larger capacity reservoir, the longer wear gives you features that you care about. So I'm sure that's true. However, it's a very -- it's a relatively easy objection to overcome, just wear the device. We can sample the product. You can wear it. I think when you put it on, you see that the load and the height of it is extremely easy to wear.

    That's why we've done the wear studies. And so we don't -- I'm sure there will be some people that may want something smaller, but the reality is when you think about the total value proposition that it represents, it's head and shoulders in terms of what's available in the market. So we think we can overcome those objections with making the product available as a starter kit and as samples to use.

    Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Richard Newitter with Truist Securities.

    Richard Newitter: Congrats on the quarter. Continuing the questions on Fit here. As we think of the gross margin impact even beyond kind of the initial launch, but including the initial period of launch, can you just give us a little bit more on how to think of the gross margin impact as this scales and you grow into the capacity? And then I have a follow-up.

    It has been revealed that chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Rich. What we've always stated about Fit is that the first year is really all about building a user base, expanding the formulary and health plan access and scaling manufacturing. So as such, in that first year, we're going to be using co-pay assistance, as you said, and other patient access programs while we build the coverage. So we've said that there will be limited impact in terms of revenue and margin for the beginning of the launch, and that's just being realistic as to what the financials look like.

    According to recent reports, and then as it scales and builds over the first 18 to 24 months, we're going to get more capacity scale, so we're going to get more margin enhancement from that. And as we get more formulary coverage, the co-pay assistance and things like that will also fall off. So we'll see increasing margins from both of those regions. So that's kind of how we see it from a scaling standpoint, going from a minimal impact to a much greater and very profitable impact over the long term.

    Sources indicate that richard Newitter: That's helpful. And then maybe just for Que. One of the questions we get just on competitive bidding and the rental model that's coming. Can you just remind us of how you are thinking about that and kind of where you have confidence on potential long-term pricing implications across your businesses?

    Que Thanh Dallara: Yes. Look, we expect that the administration will continue to press forward with competitive bidding. And I think -- in general, I think you agree that competitive bidding is not a good thing for the industry as a whole. It's -- the Medicare business for us is single-digit number of our overall business. So this is something that we expect to withstand. And so when we look at our overall portfolio, we've got MiniMed Fit going through pharmacy, our CGMs available through pharmacy. And as the pumps -- that mix goes -- increases through pharmacy, we expect that there will be price opportunities with that channel in the U.S.

    Industry observers note that we continue to advocate for choice and access with the administration with CMS as they go through the details in rolling this out. I think the rental model is still -- there are details to be figured out. Given that the devices in this space are single-use devices, renting them out is -- there are certain barriers that we have to overcome. So I think there's still details to be figured out. So we're managing this. And the fact that we have the strength of this portfolio with all these new products opening up the pharmacy channel, I think that helps us -- it provides a number of levers to offset challenges that competitive bidding may provide.

    Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Pasquale with Barclays.

    Recent findings suggest that christopher (Chris) Pasquale: I wanted to ask about Vivera. You talked a lot about choice as a key design consideration. Users can pick and choose how they interact with the algorithm, which certainly adds a lot of flexibility. But does that mean that the training required to get upcoming users comfortable with the system will be more involved than it will be for algorithms that just don't give them as many options since they've got to be comfortable with all the different ways they can use it? And how do you think about what that means for the ability of non-endocrinologists to prescribe it?

    Que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Chris. We actually designed it to be very easy to onboard onto therapy. All you need is your total daily dose. So if you're on an MDI, you know what your total daily dose is, that's all you need to enter therapy. There are no settings to be done by the physician. You don't need to do any programming. It's as close to self-start as you can get. So the training is extremely simple. So that's Vivera, and it's designed to really eliminate carb counting, but not sacrifice outcomes. So we want people to be above 70% time in range without needing to carb count whatsoever.

    It has been revealed that now a lot of the feedback we hear from patients though is when you have something like a forced full closed loop that we hear from some of our competitors, people are nervous about that because they don't know how it's going to perform. It may not get you to 70% time in range. And if you get into a sticky situation, there's not much you can do because there's no -- there aren't any levers to pull. You're in a forced full closed system. In our system, if you want tighter control, you can input and say something like, "I'm eating," or you can put in a carb count.

    Sources indicate that and the system will also take that input and give you better control. And so we've really designed it to accommodate the full spectrum: people who don't want to do anything and people who do. And one algorithm can handle all of that. And I think that actually builds trust because just like in our commentary, the car analogy, a lot of people are nervous about going to a self-driving car because it's quite a foreign concept.

    But once you're in one and you see how it works and if you can take control at any time, you're more likely to trust that system than trust your health to a forced algorithm that can only get to a certain maximum, doesn't get you out of trouble should you get into those sort of tricky corners.

    In a recent development, christopher (Chris) Pasquale: That's helpful. And then the announcement on the dual glucose-ketone sensor was an interesting update. Curious how you think about who across your user base that is going to appeal to.

    Que Thanh Dallara: Look, I think it's still early days with how to use the ketone information. I think we're very excited to be the first. We believe the first app that's going to incorporate ketone and glucose on the same screen. I think the other implementation you're going to see in the market will have 2 apps. You've got your CGM app that may have -- that will have the ketone on it and then you've got the pump app, and we're going to integrate that all into one. So I think it still is something that needs to be studied.

    In a recent development, but I think for people who want the bells and whistles and additional information, they would be attracted to the ketone sensor. We hear a lot of interest from pediatric accounts that it's sort of belts and suspenders for parents. And so, but it's still early days in terms of that user experience. There's more to be studied. But by having all that information onto the one app, I think we're simplifying the experience for providers and for patients. And I think that facilitates what else can you do with ketones and where can that be helpful into the future. But certainly, on peds accounts, for example, I think it will be a very strong value proposition with our system.

    Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Joanne Wuensch with Citi.

    Sources indicate that joanne Wuensch: It seems like the Vivera algorithm will be available after the launch of Fit. And then my second question is, is there a way to measure the percentage of revenue that's going through the pharmacy today? And is there a goal for what that might look like in the future?

    According to recent reports, que Thanh Dallara: Thanks, Joanne. On Vivera, it will be a simple over-the-air update. As you know, when you get a Flex pump, it's really less than 10 minutes to upgrade the firmware and get the latest software update, and it will be the same with MiniMed Fit as well as MiniMed Flex. So very simple over-the-air update. So as soon as Vivera is cleared, and we're preparing for launch, we can push that to all our customers and all the devices. So it's pretty seamless. In terms of the pharmacy channel, today, our pharmacy mix is relatively low in the single-digit category. We haven't given you a number. I think, obviously, we've got significant ambitions to increase that.

    We're pretty excited with Fit exclusively going through pharmacy in the U.S. And so I think as that ramps, we'll be able to share more in the future.

    Industry observers note that daniel Markowitz: Congrats on a strong update. First, I wanted to ask, really strong gross margin execution in the second quarter. And then any other thoughts you can share on the evolution of gross margins over the coming quarters and years?

    Industry observers note that chad J. Spooner: Thanks, Daniel. Yes, gross margin execution, it's really around -- the main factor is Simplera, right? We've talked about this year having the depressed margin from prior years because Simplera presently has a lower margin than our legacy and Instinct CGMs. But we have done a phenomenal job from increasing our yields even more than we expected when we released this year off. So that's a huge driver. We're seeing benefits in our warranty. So as our products get more and more reliable, our warranty costs are getting even better than we anticipated. We're seeing manufacturing variance favorability across the board and even favorable PPV. So really, it's really strong execution across everything manufacturing from a gross margin standpoint.

    So that's great news, right, from where we anticipated being. And then as we think of the evolution, we talk about all the new product releases. So as we launch new products, as we said, as they scale manufacturing-wise, they'll get more and more profitable. So Simplera is an example of something that you need to build significant scale to get to profitability, we're getting better. Flex is one where we're seeing very good conversion quickly to getting to near profitability or better than 780G given the simplicity of the bill of materials.

    As we think of the patch pump, it's going to obviously have a lower gross margin as we spoke about earlier, given the things that we're doing to get on formulary and as the scale needs to build up. So we're going to see some ebbs and flows, but it's -- that's why we always talk about our bottom line EBITDA is going to be driven consistently year in and year out by operating leverage, which we have very good control over. But you can be sure that in the years to come, our gross margin will continue to also get better as Fit and these products that we keep launching get to scale as well.

    I think that we're proving our track record of strong manufacturing and building out some of these new products and getting to better profitability faster.

    Recent findings suggest that daniel Markowitz: That's helpful. And then my follow-up, can you talk a little bit more about the organic outlook for the second half?     A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession proposal, makes it worse.

    However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a massive haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    Recent findings suggest that this lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

    Netflix Stock Is Down 37% in 2026, But the Business Is Still Growing. Here's Why I'd Buy It Before the End of November.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that media-streaming veteran Netflix (NFLX +1.32%) is on the outs with Wall Street again.
    • Industry observers note that and the more I look at the drooping stock chart, the more I scratch my head in confusion.
    • Third-quarter results did not look like those of a company in trouble.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Anders Bylund – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:07PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Netflix ›.

    Sources indicate that media-streaming veteran Netflix (NFLX +1.32%) is on the outs with Wall Street again. The stock reached all-time highs in the summer of 2025, as investors forgave the manufacturer for the canceled, expensive Warner Bros. buyout idea. As of Nov. 24, Netflix stock is down 56% from that peak, including a 37% year-to-date drop.

    Industry observers note that and the more I look at the drooping stock chart, the more I scratch my head in confusion. The business keeps growing, video streaming remains a healthy global market, and Netflix's stock isn't even expensive.

    Third-quarter results did not look like those of a company in trouble. Revenue rose 11.8% to $12.9 billion. Operating income jumped 37.3% to $4.5 billion, and operating margin widened to 34.6% from 28.2% in the year-ago period. Management guided for 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion, up 13%, and an operating margin of 31.5%, versus 29.5% in 2025. That's a combo of double-digit revenue growth and widening margins.

    According to recent reports, investors sold anyway. The stock fell as much as 6.7% the next morning, and several analysts trimmed their price targets. At first glance, the reasons look fair. Netflix cut its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from roughly $3 billion to about $2.7 billion, citing slower rollout of some latest ad products. Ad revenue is still on pace to grow more than 80% this year, per co-CEO Greg Peters. Management conceded, though, that view-hour growth needs to improve and that the U.S. content group can do better.

    It has been revealed that "Our [U.S.] engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years, but we know that we can do better. And that better is our upside," Peters said on the earnings call. "It's our goal to go from very good to great on the performance of that slate.".

    Industry observers note that now check the stock's price tag. Netflix's market cap is about $238.6 billion. Tack on $7.1 billion of net debt, and the whole enterprise costs about 15.8 times the operating income it generated over the past four quarters. That's a low multiple for a manufacturer that turned 31.3% of its revenue into operating income over the past year. Take a quick look at the price chart and you'd assume the business was shrinking. Well, it's not.

    Management has been voting with the checkbook, so to speak. Netflix bought back 63.9 million shares for $4.8 billion last quarter (a company record, narrowly edging the Q2 buyback budget) at an average of about $75 per stub. The stock now sits around $59, so the timing could have been better. Still, $22.3 billion of buyback authorization remains, against $8.2 billion of cash and about $12.0 billion of expected 2026 free cash flow. Netflix has leaned harder into buybacks as the stock has slid this year, and the remaining authorization leaves room for more:.

    Sources indicate that NFLX data by YCharts. The chart shows quarterly buybacks; Netflix reported $4.8 billion for Q3 2026.

    Wall Street has not given up on the story. The analyst consensus rating is Buy, and short-sellers hold roughly 2% of Netflix's shares, a thin bearish bet against the stock.

    According to recent reports, the fourth quarter should keep the content engine busy. Netflix calls it the biggest quarterly live slate it has ever scheduled, including its first NFL Thanksgiving Eve game on Nov. 25. That game kicks off a stretch of live events that could shift sentiment fast: a Christmas Day football doubleheader and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua heavyweight boxing event. Self-produced entertainment releases include "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a new season of "The Diplomat," and the sixth and final run of "Emily in Paris.".

    Netflix also looks to launch its advertising tier in 15 more countries next year, starting in March. It recently named former Disney (DIS +1.86%) executive Peter Rice as chief content officer. Regional hits matter, too; Netflix has a deep bench of local producers, and their reveals are moving the needle. For instance, India view hours grew 24% in the third quarter while revenue there rose about 18% on a currency-neutral basis.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Sources indicate that I can't pretend that Netflix is a risk-free investment. Some latest ad products are behind schedule. Fourth-quarter margin guidance of 26% absorbs about 120 basis points of cost from headcount cuts. Operating income is guided to about $3.5 billion, up 18.4% from a year ago, and that's a sharp slowdown from the third quarter's 37.3% jump. The U.S. slate needs to start landing home runs instead of base hits, which is exactly the job Peter Rice just inherited. So no, you shouldn't bet the farm, the cat, and the horse it rode in on. A normal slice of a diversified portfolio is plenty.

    Industry observers note that but a growing, cash-generating business at about 16 times operating income, with a Buy consensus and almost nobody shorting it? That's why I'd buy Netflix now, rather than wait for the holiday slate to change the market mood. The stock may keep sliding in the short term; the business, so far, is not.

    Most Stocks Are Losers. Here's How You Can Still Win

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It's a sobering statement, but one that's borne out by decades of stock market returns.
    • Sources indicate that research from J.P.
    • Worse still, roughly 40% of stocks had negative absolute returns.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Joe Tenebruso – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:21PM EST.

    Many of your stocks are likely to disappoint you.

    It's a sobering statement, but one that's borne out by decades of stock market returns.

    Sources indicate that research from J.P. Morgan going back to 1980 shows that two-thirds of the stocks in the Russell 3000, which is designed to track the performance of the largest 3,000 publicly traded U.S. companies, tend to underperform the index.

    Worse still, roughly 40% of stocks had negative absolute returns.

    Moreover, a report from Trivariate Research suggests that an even larger percentage of companies underperformed in recent years, with just 23% of stocks beating the S&P 500 over the past decade.

    At first glance, this data is pretty disheartening. Investing may not be easy, but this research makes it seem nearly impossible to be successful.

    The truth, fortunately, is that it's not.

    There's a beautiful asymmetry to investing.

    It's true that a stock could lose 100% of its value. Enduring such a loss is not pleasant. But a well-chosen stock can gain 200%, 500%, or even 1,000% or more.

    This capped downside and uncapped upside is part of the magic of investing. As long as you don't use leverage (such as buying stocks on margin), a few big winners can more than make up for a host of losers.

    While the odds may be against you, it's still possible to find stocks that go on to outperform the market averages.

    The most valuable suggestion I can give you is to buy shares in the best businesses you can find.

    Recent findings suggest that search for companies with the strongest competitive advantages and largest growth opportunities. This includes those with proven business models, beloved brands, superior products and services, and excellent management. Even better if they also possess powerful network effects, high barriers to entry, and sizable switching costs.

    Look for the innovators, disruptors, and best of breed. I call these businesses Tier 1 enterprises, and finding just a handful of them can set you up for a lifetime of investment success.

    Recent findings suggest that to achieve those life-changing returns, you'll need to keep them long enough to maximize their impact on your wealth. This is one reason why Warren Buffett claims his "favorite holding period is forever.".

    Strive to purchase only shares of businesses you plan to hold for many years. This will lead you to focus on companies with the strongest competitive positions and widest economic moats, or those you believe will eventually build them.

    Sources indicate that still, despite your best efforts, you will make mistakes. Don't let them derail you.

    Industry observers note that A stock you thought was a sure winner will fail. Recessions will slow the greatest of growth stories. Bear markets will bring fear, uncertainty, and doubt. Even your own emotions may betray you.

    Come what may, don't quit. Steel yourself with the knowledge that the hard times will pass and you will get through them.

    Industry observers note that learn from your mistakes. Apply the lessons to your future stock selections.

    Continuously refine your investing process until you obtain the results you need to provide for yourself and your family and achieve your financial freedom.

    By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 24, 2026 at 7:26PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    Industry observers note that shares of Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) reached a 52-week high on Oct. 6, but they have dropped by a remarkable 31% since then, as investors pressed the panic button for multiple reasons.

    Industry observers note that co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation (before he was reinstated on Nov. 23), an investigation into Nvidia's dealings in China, and a reported probe by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) into the company's accounting practices have sent the stock packing over the past month and a half. The negativity surrounding Nvidia stock was so severe that even its quarterly results and better-than-expected guidance didn't arrest its slide.

    However, Nvidia rallied over 31% following Huang’s reappointment, suggesting that investor confidence in the stock could improve. What’s more, the last time Nvidia witnessed such a sharp pullback in a short period, it went on a multi-year rally. Let's take a look at what happened in 2018.

    Nvidia stock fell 54% between October and December 2018. This massive slide was triggered by an oversupply in the graphics processing unit (GPU) market, driven by a drop in cryptocurrency-related sales. Additionally, the company was caught up in a broader sell-off of tech stocks at the time.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    According to recent reports, nvidia's growth slowed as crypto-driven GPU demand faded, leaving the organization with excess inventory. In fact, Nvidia's revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2019 (which ended in January 2019) fell 24% year over year to $2.2 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings dropped by 53% from the year-ago period during the quarter.

    Recent findings suggest that investors decided to book profits in Nvidia stock following stellar returns in 2016 and 2017. Nvidia lost 31% of its value in 2018. For comparison, it jumped by 227% in 2016 and 82% in 2017. So, this isn't the first time that Nvidia stock has lost its wheels and undergone a significant correction in a short time.

    However, what's worth noting is that Nvidia went on a stunning bull run starting in 2019, driven by multiple catalysts, including strong GPU sales during the novel coronavirus pandemic and the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in late 2022. Nvidia stock has jumped by a whopping 4,740% since the beginning of 2019.

    According to recent reports, so, savvy investors who saw the long-term opportunity in Nvidia's shares at that time are sitting on massive gains right now, even after the stock's recent sell-off. What's more, a closer look at Nvidia's valuation suggests that it is way more attractive right now than it was in 2018.

    According to recent reports, nvidia traded at less than 18 times earnings at the end of 2018. The stock at the moment has a price-to-earnings ratio of 17.7, close to the level it traded at eight years ago. The forward earnings multiple of just 10 suggests that Nvidia is on track to deliver healthy bottom-line growth.

    Meanwhile, the stock's price/earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio was just 0.31 at the end of 2018. This is a forward-looking valuation metric that's calculated by dividing a stock's trailing earnings multiple by the projected annual earnings per share (EPS) growth over the long run, let's say for five years. A PEG ratio below 1 means that the stock is undervalued when its growth potential is considered.

    Sources indicate that so, Nvidia was significantly undervalued at that time, just like it is right now. The stock right now has a PEG ratio of just 0.19, which means that investors are getting an even better deal than in 2018. But should they take this opportunity to buy shares given recent developments at the company?

    Investors are most likely in a classic dilemma right now. Nvidia's valuation suggests that the stock is a screaming buy, especially given its solid fundamentals, healthy growth, and sunny prospects.

    Industry observers note that the company reported impressive year-over-year revenue growth of 103% in the third quarter of fiscal 2027 to $115.8 billion. Adjusted earnings per share shot up by 111% to $2.68. The numbers easily exceeded consensus EPS expectations of $2.48 and the $109.1 billion revenue estimate. The company expects $130 billion in revenue in the current quarter, a 91% jump over last year and well ahead of the $125.1 billion Wall Street estimate.

    Notably, analysts have raised their EPS expectations for Nvidia, indicating continued confidence in the tech giant's prospects.

    NVDA EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts.

    Sources indicate that even the 12-month median price target of $232 implies a 41% jump, according to CNN. So, investors with a higher risk appetite who have investable cash after paying their bills, clearing expensive loans, and saving for a rainy day can consider buying this semiconductor stock. That's because Nvidia could go on a massive bull run, fueled by Huang’s comeback and the solid growth that it is poised to deliver, which could lead the market to reward it with a higher valuation in the future.

    In a recent development, after all, Nvidia sees tremendous opportunity in the AI infrastructure market, and it is making solid progress in emerging niches, such as physical AI. However, the ongoing regulatory troubles the manufacturer faces suggest it may be wise for conservative investors to wait on the sidelines.

    Tech Report: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
    • Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
    • The much more widely held B shares closed at upcoming highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

    Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

    The much more widely held B shares closed at upcoming highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

    The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

    Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

    Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

    After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

    They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

    Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

    We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the tech giant's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

    It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

    As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

    On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

    Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

    If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

    The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the tech giant as "banks, insurance, and finance.".

    The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

    Sources indicate that barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

    In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to promptly disclose any sales.

    Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

    That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

    The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

    Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

    Sources indicate that in the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

    All those numbers exclude the organization's buybacks of its own stock.

    In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway claims it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

    Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

    It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

    In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

    Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

    WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

    You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

    Recent findings suggest that two of the — well, all of the vital ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

    One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

    Industry observers note that and the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

    And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds.".

    10 stocks we like better than Shopify ›.

    Industry observers note that shopify (SHOP -1.48%) stock climbed around 9% on Monday, Nov. 23, closing at $134.30. Still, shares are down about 17% in 2026, and they'd have to rise about 33% to get back to the $179.22 record hit on Oct. 12.

    The holiday shopping season, normally the e-commerce firm's biggest stretch of the year, kicks off with Black Friday on Nov. 27.

    Sources indicate that at roughly $134 per share as I write, $5,000 buys about 37 shares. By my math, those shares might be worth about $6,800 at the end of 2030. That'd be a gain of about $1,800, or roughly 8% a year.

    Sources indicate that the estimate has Shopify's free cash flow per share more than doubling by 2030, even as growth cools. It also assumes investors will pay far less for every dollar of that cash flow than they do today, at about 65 times free cash flow.

    Industry observers note that after two straight quarters of 34% growth earlier in 2026, Shopify's revenue climbed 32% year over year in the third quarter, to around $3.7 billion. Management sees growth at a low-thirties percentage rate again in the fourth quarter, with gross profit growing at a high-twenties rate.

    In a recent development, free cash flow (the cash left after capital spending) has mostly kept pace with revenue, because Shopify's free cash flow margin hasn't changed much. Shopify kept 18% of its revenue as free cash flow in 2024 and 17% in 2025. Over the last four quarters, the number was around 19%, helped by a 22% third quarter. Management expects the fourth-quarter margin to match the 19% it reported a year before.

    It has been revealed that if fourth-quarter revenue rises around 31% at that margin, Shopify would finish 2026 with about $15.3 billion in revenue, up 32% from 2025, and about $2.9 billion in free cash flow, up around 40%. Spread over the third quarter's 1.29 billion diluted shares, that's around $2.20 of free cash flow per share.

    The share count has been dropping, too. Shopify bought back around $2.5 billion of its stock in the first nine months of 2026, and its third-quarter diluted share count was down about 2% from a year earlier.

    I've assumed revenue growth keeps slowing, from the low 30s now to the mid-teens by 2030, averaging about 20% a year from 2027 through 2030. That would put 2030 revenue around $32 billion, about twice this year's likely total.

    It has been revealed that if free cash flow holds just below 19% of revenue, where it should land in 2026, Shopify would produce almost $6 billion of it in 2030. And I've kept the share count near 1.29 billion, though buybacks have been lowering it. That puts 2030 free cash flow at around $4.60 per share, a little over twice this year's $2.20.

    Sources indicate that shopify's market cap is about $173 billion at $134.30, putting the shares at about 65 times free cash flow. At its October record, Shopify fetched about 98 times free cash flow. And even at its lowest close in 2026, about $95 on May 13, it went for roughly 59 times free cash flow.

    I've assumed 40 times free cash flow at the end of 2030. That's still a premium price, and it looks fair for a business that could be growing in the mid-teens by then. But it's far below anything investors have paid for Shopify this year.

    In a recent development, at 40 times free cash flow, $4.60 per share gives a stock price around $184. Thirty-seven shares at that price are worth about $6,800.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    In a recent development, of course, another free cash flow multiple would change the result a lot. If investors still paid 65 times free cash flow in 2030, the $5,000 would grow to about $11,100. At 30 times free cash flow, it would be worth about $5,100, barely more than what went in.

    In a recent development, shopify's business looks healthy enough to keep growing its cash flow at an impressive rate. But my base case comes out to roughly 8% a year, and a less generous valuation in 2030 might erase most of that gain. This year alone, shares have closed as low as about $95 and as high as about $179.

    With swings like that, I'd want a lower starting price before putting $5,000 into Shopify stock.

    It has been revealed that tech stocks slid again on Tuesday, and some of the market's most famous investors have been positioning for that kind of drop. Quarterly filings show that two billionaire-run firms added big bets against the Nasdaq-100 during the third quarter.

    The bets use put options, which give the holder the right to sell at a set price and generally rise in value when the underlying investment falls. The filings, called 13Fs, were made with the SEC on Nov. 16 and show holdings as of Sept. 30.

    Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

    It has been revealed that paul Singer's Elliott Investment Management held puts on 5.46 million shares of the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -1.99%), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, according to its latest 13F. The filing values them at $4.04 billion, with only its Phillips 66 and Triple Flag Precious Metals stakes representing a bigger value.

    It has been revealed that importantly, that figure is the value of the shares the puts cover, rather than what Elliott paid for them or what it could make. The filing doesn't show the strike prices or expiration dates, so the size of the actual bet is unknown.

    Sources indicate that three months earlier, Elliott held puts on 3.48 million QQQ shares, valued at $2.56 billion, according to its prior filing. It also raised its puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -7.26%) to 800,000 shares from 250,000, covering $487 million of shares.

    But Elliott isn't only betting against tech. It also reported puts covering $1.27 billion of an industrials fund, $903 million of a consumer staples fund, and $865 million of a gold miners fund. It cut its puts on a technology-software fund nearly in half, to $873 million. As a whole, the spread looks more like protection across the whole market than a single bet against tech.

    According to recent reports, paul Tudor Jones' Tudor Investment held QQQ puts covering 8.55 million shares valued at $6.32 billion, according to its 13F. That's up from 4.74 million shares, or $3.49 billion, in its prior filing.

    However, Tudor also raised its QQQ calls, which gain when the fund rises, to 7.75 million shares, or $5.74 billion. So its puts outweigh its calls, but not by much. Its biggest bearish line wasn't tech at all: puts on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks smaller companies, covering $8.75 billion of shares.

    Separately, Stanley Druckenmiller isn't betting against tech, but he isn't betting on it either. He told the TomorrowX conference in Austin this month that he's "taking a break" from stocks and is close to neutral on equities while he waits for a clearer outlook.

    According to recent reports, not much. These filings have real limits. Besides omitting strike prices and costs, a 13F doesn't show short sales or positions in securities outside U.S.-listed securities. A put can be an outright bet on a decline, or it can be insurance for a firm that owns a lot of stocks. Both Elliott and Tudor hold billions in other positions that those puts may be protecting.

    According to recent reports, the data is also somewhat stale. The filings show positions as of Sept. 30, and these firms trade often. Any of them could have changed by now.

    What the filings do show is that experienced investors are paying for protection, especially against tech stocks and the broader Nasdaq. For long-term investors, the takeaway isn't to sell. Instead, check how much of the portfolio rides on a handful of names (particularly AI names), and make sure it's an amount they can live with if selling continues.
