    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, the average price of a can of soda in the U.S. is around $0.60 when bought as part of a 12-pack -- up 80% from its price in 2019. While this is an extreme example, it highlights the devastating impact inflation can have on your purchasing power and the real value of your stock market returns.

    Unfortunately for investors, inflation remains a problem. And a devastating warning from President Donald Trump suggests it could get worse before it gets better. Let's dig deeper into the market's challenges and discuss strategies investors can use to stay ahead of the curve.

    Sources indicate that for many investors, the Trump era has been a bit of a headscratcher. The administration has deliberately pursued disruptive policies, such as massive tariffs that can make it harder for many U.S. companies to do business. But instead of crashing, stocks have gone gangbusters, with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.50%) jumping 25% since his election victory in November.

    To be fair, some of this is luck. Trump has been in the right place at the right time to oversee the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), which has single-handedly added trillions to the value of America's tech industry. That mentioned, White House policies have also played a role.

    Trump's One Major Beautiful Bill Act helped lock in corporate tax cuts while also slashing regulations in the energy industry and introducing goodies such as allowing companies to write off certain categories of research and development expenses for tax purposes. Big tech is also happy with the administration's generally pro-AI stance, which is crucial at a time when public pushback against data center construction is growing.

    Recent findings suggest that that said, while Trump has managed to keep Wall Street happy so far, the administration has struggled to rein in other macroeconomic challenges that could undermine investor returns over the long haul. The biggest challenge is inflation. Tariffs and the Iran war have helped push the U.S. inflation rate to around 4% as of October, which is well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.

    Higher inflation hurts investors' real returns and encourages the central bank to continue raising interest rates. This generally hurts stock valuations by making it harder for businesses to access the capital they need to invest in future growth.

    Image source: Official White House Photo.

    When asked about the situation earlier last month, Trump's response was alarming. In an interview with Time magazine, he suggested "certain levels of inflation" could help pay down the national debt "very rapidly." The logic may be that by lowering the value of the dollar, inflation will also devalue America's $40 trillion in borrowings, making it easier to manage. These remarks suggest the White House is willing to tolerate high inflation for much longer than investors will be comfortable with.

    Trump's warning suggests that the U.S. government doesn't have a strong blueprint to bring down inflation or manage the national debt. In fact, both of these problems could get worse over the coming months as the war in Iran (along with the war in Ukraine) continues to drive up military spending and create lasting bottlenecks in the global economy.

    Sources indicate that that mentioned, this isn't the time to panic. And it can pay to look toward the wisdom of investing legend Warren Buffett, who advised investors to never bet against America in his annual shareholder letter during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. Over the long haul, the country has consistently bounced back from crises only to emerge stronger than ever. And there is no reason to assume this time will be the exception.

    The recent midterm results have also already eased fears in the oil markets, as many traders expect the newly introduced Democrat-controlled Congress to impose more checks and balances on Trump's foreign policy.

    Recent findings suggest that the economic situation remains uncertain, but the long-term outlook is bright. And investors can stay ahead by increasing portfolio diversification to avoid being overly exposed to underperformance in any specific asset class.

    • It has been revealed that this, despite the Cavs coming in with a rest advantage, with the Bulls on the second night of a back-to-back after going to overtime against the Nuggets on Sunday.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Chicago Bulls entered Thanksgiving week as one of the NBA's worst teams: 4-12, getting outscored by nearly eight points per 100 possessions, with the second-worst defense in the NBA. And yet, they controlled the bulk of Monday's matchup with the Cleveland Cavaliers, leading for nearly the entire final three quarters — and by as many as 24 points — in a 122-108 win.

    It has been revealed that this, despite the Cavs coming in with a rest advantage, with the Bulls on the second night of a back-to-back after going to overtime against the Nuggets on Sunday. And despite Chicago being without leading scorer Norman Powell, who's stuck in street clothes nursing a strained right hamstring, and 2026 lottery pick Caleb Wilson, out with a broken right hand. And despite a pair of Chicago starters — point guard Josh Giddey and swingman Matas Buzelis — getting benched, again, late in the fourth quarter by first-year head coach Tiago Splitter, who elected to close with backup point guard Tre Jones and intriguing two-way reserve Jaylin Sellers. (Giddey did not seem particularly pleased about that.).

    And, perhaps most importantly, despite the Cavs … well, frankly, they're just supposed to be better than this.

    Donovan Mitchell (right), James Harden and the Cleveland Cavaliers have stumbled to .500 a month into the season.

    Yes, Cleveland's without Evan Mobley, an integral component of its operations on both sides of the floor. And yes, Kenny Atkinson's club wound up on the business end of Chicago going 20-for-49 from 3-point range while the Cavs made just eight of their 31 triple tries. Not exactly easy to win when you're outscored by 36 points from long distance.

    It's not just the simple, cruel vicissitudes of shooting variance, though. Aside from Mobley, the Cavs had the entire rest of their preferred rotation against a four-win team … and they still got drilled. A Cleveland squad that made it to the Eastern Conference finals last spring enters Wednesday's matchup with the Newly introduced York Knicks — the team that, as you might recall, annihilated the Cavs in that series en route to winning the NBA championship — at 9-9, in seventh place in the East.

    In a recent development, that's a long way from where the Cavs — one of the most expensive rosters in the sport — want to be … and, from the sound of things, they've got some pretty significant questions to answer before they can get there. From Danny Cunningham of The Inside Shot:.

    Donovan Mitchell, who had a game-high 28 points, was asked about the effort being inconsistent from quarter-to-quarter or game-to-game this season.

    Mitchell thought for a full five seconds after the question was asked.

    Recent findings suggest that "I think," he said before pausing for eight more seconds. "I'm trying to figure out how not to end up on ESPN.".

    According to recent reports, "I think the biggest thing now is just figuring each other out. We're not here in the locker room panicking, and all I can say to that, is what we got going forward. Nights like tonight are bad. It's a bad night, and we got to respond to that. We've got to respond to that and just keep playing our game. There's so many different things you can point to, but at the end of the day for us, it's within us. I have all the confidence in everybody in here, and we've got all the confidence in each other. We've got to go out there and execute it. That doesn't really answer your question, but yeah.".

    Sources indicate that if there's one thing I'm qualified to assess as a longtime professional blogger, it's this: That was a lot of words to not really make any point or address the issue at hand. Which, come to think of it, might constitute a pretty loud statement about the state of affairs in Cleveland right about now.

    It has been revealed that mitchell wasn't the only Cavalier searching for an answer to the issues that have characterized the club's fits-and-starts opening to the season. Peyton Watson, the swingman who came over from Denver in an offseason sign-and-trade intended to plug Cleveland's long-yawning hole on the wing, offered a somewhat more direct answer than the All-NBA scoring guard.

    "I think if we knew the answer, we would just do it," Watson stated in the locker room. "I think we're still searching for that. You know, I'm always trying to communicate with my teammates and try to help make their job easier and just be a guy that connects the team in a lot of ways. I think I try to just go out there and lead by example by playing as hard as I can every night. I just think that everybody has got to look inward and look themselves in the mirror and ask themselves, 'Am I giving it 100% every single night?' I think that if that's not the case, then we need to go to the drawing board and really, like I said, look in the mirror and evaluate ourselves.".

    That doesn't exactly seem like the most stirring vote of confidence for the competitive makeup of the Cavaliers, especially considering they've already gone through a few moments that would seem to invite such sober self-reflection.

    Blowing a 29-point lead against the 76ers on opening night. Dropping both ends of a home-and-home to the post-injury-apocalypse Thunder. Getting boat-raced by the Knicks in the second half at home, an extension of the pain of the conference finals. Getting blown out by a Hornets team playing without Brandon Miller or Kon Knueppel. Getting out-executed down the stretch by a Grizzlies squad playing without Ty Jerome. And now, Monday's scattershot effort in Chicago.

    It just feels like something's missing in Cleveland, some spark, some urgency — and it starts on the defensive end.

    It has been revealed that the last half-decade of success for the Cavs — a climb out of the post-LeBron basement that began with the Mobley/Allen/Darius Garland unit under J.B. Bickerstaff, and that continued after the trade for Mitchell made it a "core four" — had been predicated on consistently stout defenses, with Cleveland ranking in the top eight in points allowed per possession each season from 2021 through 2025. That began to shift when Atkinson's arrival supercharged the offense, and more firmly tilted after dealing for Harden; Cleveland posted a top-five offense after the trade deadline, but a below-average defense, and got routinely torched by the Knicks in the four-game conference finals sweep.

    Industry observers note that the Cavs now sit at 21st in defensive efficiency — on pace for their first bottom-10 finish on that end since 2020-21. They're conceding shots at the rim and from beyond the 3-point line more regularly, and they give up wide-open 3s at a bottom-10 rate. (Nearly half of Chicago's 3-point attempts on Monday came without a Cavalier defender within 6 feet of the shooter.) They don't force turnovers, and they're average-at-best at clearing the defensive glass and guarding without fouling. That's a recipe for underwhelming results, unless you can balance out that bottom-10 defense with a No. 1-with-a-bullet offense … which the Cavs, currently a good-but-not-overwhelming seventh in points scored per possession, don't have at the moment.

    Maybe they will. Get Mobley healthy, get Harden — who followed up his 51-point Friday masterclass by shooting 5-for-14 from the floor with seven turnovers in Chicago — more consistently off the schneid, and get Watson (a career-low 48% on 2-pointers and 27% on 3s) thawed out, and maybe these Cavs have the ingredients they need to build on last season's trip to the final four and put themselves in position to make a bid to represent the East in the NBA Finals. They believe they have the talent to do that.

    Sources indicate that right now, though, they feel like a team that's less than the sum of its parts — a group that's playing like it's just kind of going through the motions until the real season starts, rather than one that needs to earn its postseason spot in an East that's gotten more crowded at the top. And if the Cavs want to have a shot at being the last team standing come springtime, they need to start finding answers as fall turns to winter.

    Industry observers note that "You can't just turn it on in April or May," Cavs guard Sam Merrill told reporters. "I think building the right habits only makes it easier to play that way once you get to later in the season and in the playoffs. We continue to talk about it. That's got to continue to be our mindset.".

    Sources indicate that talking about it is one thing. Their next chance to do something about it comes Wednesday in Upcoming York. One bit of good news for Mitchell and Co., at least? The game won't air on ESPN.

    Anthropic Has Plunged 30% From Its Peak. Here’s the Price at Which I’d Buy.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Following months of anticipation, artificial intelligence (AI) developer Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) made its public market debut on Nov.
    • Indeed, Anthropic's revenue is growing at an extraordinary rate.
    • Let's explore what's driving the sell-off in Anthropic stock and assess the valuation at which the organization could become a compelling investment.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Adam Spatacco – Nov 24, 2026 at 8:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Following months of anticipation, artificial intelligence (AI) developer Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) made its public market debut on Nov. 19. While the maker of Claude initially received an enthusiastic reception, the excitement has been short-lived. Less than a week after going public, Anthropic stock has already started selling off.

    Indeed, Anthropic's revenue is growing at an extraordinary rate. But smart investors are not overlooking the capital-intensive nature underpinning the company's expansion. Furthermore, competition across the large language model (LLM) landscape raises important questions about Anthropic's path to profitability.

    Let's explore what's driving the sell-off in Anthropic stock and assess the valuation at which the organization could become a compelling investment.

    Anthropic completed the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, surpassing the $75 billion raised by Space Exploration Technologies back in June. Including the full exercise of the underwriters' option to purchase additional shares, Anthropic's IPO generated $93.5 billion in gross proceeds.

    The company also completed a concurrent $26 billion private placement involving Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, and Micron Technology. Combined gross proceeds from the two transactions reached $119.5 billion.

    According to recent reports, when Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq, shares opened at $111.50, or about 34% above the offering price of $83. Shares subsequently climbed to an intraday high of $115.10 before reversing course and closing their first day of trading at $97.17. As of this writing (Nov. 24), Anthropic stock is hovering around $80, representing a decline of 30% from its high.

    Some of the selling pressure likely reflects momentum traders locking in profits, but attributing the entire decline to short-term trading overlooks several important fundamental concerns.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Anthropic's growth is difficult to dispute. According to its S-1 filing, the company generated approximately $17 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing 1,127% growth year over year. Furthermore, Anthropic ended October with an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion.

    According to recent reports, revenue growth is only one part of Anthropic's financial profile. The organization has $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments, including $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before Dec. 31, 2030.

    While these obligations shouldn't be confused with conventional debt, they illustrate the capital requirements required to develop and operate frontier AI models. Anthropic's ability to generate sustainable profits depends heavily on whether customer demand and premium pricing can justify these investments.

    In a recent development, anthropic competes against OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's Gemini, Meta's Muse, and an expanding ecosystem of open-weight models. As generative models become more sophisticated and less expensive to operate, Anthropic may face pressure to lower its prices while continuing to invest aggressively in computing capacity.

    Industry observers note that unlike Alphabet or Meta Platforms, Anthropic doesn't have a mature, highly profitable advertising or cloud computing business that generates cash to help subsidize its AI infrastructure investments. As a result, investors are being asked to place enormous amounts of faith in Anthropic's ability to translate its revenue growth into durable earnings and free cash flow at some point in the future.

    Given Anthropic's lack of profitability, a traditional price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio isn't particularly useful in this analysis. Instead, I'd value the company relative to its annualized revenue run rate. At $80 per share, Anthropic's market capitalization is roughly $1.1 trillion. This equates to 13.5 times its annualized revenue run rate from October.

    I am more interested in Anthropic stock at $50 per share. At that price, the company would boast an implied market cap of about $690 billion, equivalent to 8.5 times its annualized revenue run rate. Anthropic's growth could allow the company to grow into this valuation relatively swiftly. For example, if its annualized revenue run rate doubles to roughly $160 billion, a $690 billion valuation would represent just 4.3 times that figure.

    Sources indicate that with that noted, investors shouldn't assume Anthropic's current growth trajectory will last indefinitely. Moreover, the manufacturer will need to demonstrate that its revenue can fuel sustainable free cash flow despite its infrastructure commitments.

    In a recent development, although Anthropic is one of the most premier businesses leading the AI revolution, an exciting company doesn't always make an attractive stock at every price. At $50 per share, I'd be more comfortable initiating a modest position and gradually building exposure as Anthropic makes progress toward profitability. Until then, I think patience is warranted.

    This AI Chip Stock Just Crashed 38% on a Memory Shortage Warning. Its Filings Flagged the Risk Months Ago

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ambarella (AMBA -19.96%) shares plummeted 38% to $27 in after-hours trading Tuesday after the chipmaker warned that a worldwide memory shortage is hurting demand for its products.
    • Ambarella makes low-power chips that run artificial intelligence directly on devices such as security cameras, car safety systems, drones and dashcams.
    • According to recent reports, but what spooked investors were the projections: For the fourth quarter, which ends Jan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 24, 2026 at 6:27PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Ambarella ›.

    It has been revealed that ambarella (AMBA -19.96%) shares plummeted 38% to $27 in after-hours trading Tuesday after the chipmaker warned that a worldwide memory shortage is hurting demand for its products. Nasdaq halted trading in the stock at 4:01 p.m. ET ahead of the news.

    Ambarella makes low-power chips that run artificial intelligence directly on devices such as security cameras, car safety systems, drones and dashcams. Revenue for the third quarter, which ended Oct. 31, rose 6% to $115.2 million, while adjusted earnings rose to $0.28 per share from $0.27 a year earlier.

    According to recent reports, but what spooked investors were the projections: For the fourth quarter, which ends Jan. 31, Ambarella expects revenue of $70 million to $75 million. That's a drop of 35% to 39% from the quarter it just reported.

    In a recent development, "The unprecedented rise in memory prices and the scarcity of memory supply we previously highlighted has intensified and is causing many customers to reduce their outlooks," CEO Fermi Wang said in the release. He added that third-quarter revenue landed at the low end of the company's guidance range because consumer device sales came in below expectations.

    Ambarella doesn't make memory, but almost every device that uses its chips also needs memory chips. When memory becomes scarce and expensive, the camera and car electronics makers that buy from Ambarella build fewer products or delay them, and they order fewer Ambarella chips.

    Ambarella isn't the only company feeling it this week. Hewlett Packard Enterprise CEO Antonio Neri said on Monday's earnings call that he expects memory supply to stay constrained until at least the second half of 2028. On Tuesday, HP Inc. said in its earnings release that it is "taking steps to address memory and storage cost pressures.".

    Ambarella guided for adjusted operating expenses of $57.5 million to $59.5 million in the fourth quarter, with an adjusted gross margin of 59% to 60.25%. At the midpoints, that works out to about $43 million in gross profit against roughly $58.5 million in expenses, resulting in an adjusted operating loss of about $15 million. Using the firm's third-quarter figures, which leave out stock-based compensation and acquisition costs the same way its guidance does, Ambarella earned an adjusted operating profit of about $11 million.

    The company expects to keep its overall spending roughly level even as revenue drops, and it has the cash to do so. It ended the quarter with $282.8 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, up from $272.3 million three months earlier.

    Sources indicate that ambarella had been flagging the problem for months. Its March annual report listed memory shortages as a possibility. By its June quarterly report, it said there "have been tightening supply conditions in the memory market." In September's quarterly report, it added that tighter memory supply "could have an impact on" customers' demand for its products.

    According to recent reports, the earnings release 8-K that came out a day earlier didn't mention memory specifically at all. It forecast third-quarter revenue of $115 million to $124 million. Ambarella came in at $115.2 million, the bottom of that range.

    Wang tried to separate the shortage from the long-term story. Memory problems "do not have an impact on our very positive secular growth outlook for edge AI," he remarked, and he expects the tech giant's fiscal 2028, which begins in February, "to be a growth year.".

    It has been revealed that that's a claim worth assessing. Ambarella states many of its customers are lowering their outlooks while memory stays scarce and expensive, and if HPE's view holds, that may not ease until at least the second half of 2028. Wang also stated edge AI revenue hit a record in the third quarter, so the demand for AI on devices is real. The question is how long the memory squeeze keeps it from turning into sales.

    It has been revealed that for investors in semiconductor stocks, Ambarella's warning is a reminder that the AI boom comes at a cost to companies outside the data center, with the same memory demand that's filling orders for AI servers draining supply from smaller device makers. Until Ambarella demonstrates its revenue can recover, its stock is likely to trade on headlines about memory prices (as HPE and Dell did on Tuesday), and buyers looking for a turnaround in AI may want to wait for next quarter's guidance.

    When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 796%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 200% for the S&P 500.

    #188115. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (517 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex.
    • With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.
    • Recent findings suggest that implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting significant moves.

    With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

    Recent findings suggest that implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

    "Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, stated in a text ahead of the tech giant's after-market report on Tuesday.

    Recent findings suggest that since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is presently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

    The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

    One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

    With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

    By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

    Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (265 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the manufacturer "has its own China problem.".
    • Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
    • Recent findings suggest that the report claims that "after the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the manufacturer "has its own China problem.".

    Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

    Recent findings suggest that the report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the organization kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers.".

    CNBC did not independently verify this information.

    Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips.".

    The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

    Industry observers note that "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson stated in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.".

    Sources indicate that lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

    AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.
